standard.title: Improvise, devise and interpret drama
standard.description: improvise and devise drama and/or interpret scripted drama, manipulating elements of drama and applying conventions relevant to the style/form
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can use elements of drama and simple conventions in own drama work (AC9ADR6C01). They have not yet selected and manipulated elements with clear rationale for how each serves the intended dramatic action, nor applied style-specific conventions with deliberate intent.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students improvise, devise and interpret drama where manipulation of elements and application of conventions is deliberate and connected to intended dramatic action and meaning.

nodes.label: Identifying and developing dramatic potential
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify dramatic potential in a starting point and develop it into dramatic action using elements of drama
nodes.minimum_width: Identify dramatic potential in a given starting point (stimulus, text, image, scenario); develop it into a short dramatic action using at least one element of drama deliberately
nodes.typical_width: Identify dramatic potential in diverse starting points; use improvisation to explore situations, characters and relationships; develop dramatic action using elements of drama with a clear purpose
wider: Use 'mantle of the expert' or play-building to develop dramatic action from an inquiry question — evaluate how the collaborative devising process constrains and enables dramatic choices
Respond to the dramatic potential of an image using the questions 'What's happening? What has happened? What's going to happen next?' — develop improvised scenes from each response
Identify dramatic potential in research or issues and use improvisation to develop situations and characters that represent multiple perspectives on the issue

response_modes.reason: Students need to build a repertoire of starting points — stimulus types, devising approaches, dramatic structures — before they can identify and develop dramatic potential reliably. Each approach (mantle of the expert, image response, play-building, inquiry question) produces different kinds of dramatic material and builds different generative skills.

success_criteria: Identifies dramatic potential in a given starting point
Develops it into dramatic action using at least one element deliberately
Dramatic action has a clear direction — not just loosely connected scenes

nodes.label: Manipulating elements and applying conventions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can manipulate elements of drama and apply style-relevant conventions to shape and communicate dramatic action
nodes.minimum_width: Manipulate at least one element of drama (e.g. tension, symbol, space) and apply at least one convention with a clear reason; explain how each shapes the dramatic action
nodes.typical_width: Manipulate a range of elements and apply conventions relevant to the style or form; use voice, movement, space and time to heighten tension, focus action and shape meaning; document and justify choices
wider: Employ voice/vocalisation and movement to heighten tension and shape meaning — develop an extended sequence where multiple element manipulations build toward a dramatic climax
Apply conventions such as flashback, aside, slow motion or chorus — evaluate how each convention shapes what the audience understands about time, character and situation

Work collaboratively to interpret scripted drama — use improvisation to explore characters and relationships, apply conventions, block the performance space — evaluate how each decision changes the meaning

response_modes.reason: Students commonly apply elements and conventions by default — using the familiar rather than the purposeful. Working across multiple styles, forms and dramatic contexts — devised, scripted, collaborative, solo — forces students to develop the habit of purposeful element manipulation rather than defaulting to comfortable choices.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The scripted drama interpretation direction — using improvisation to explore characters, blocking space, applying conventions — is genuinely rich collaborative problem-solving that goes well beyond minimum element manipulation. Students who engage here develop directorial thinking alongside performative thinking.
success_criteria: Manipulates at least one element with a clear reason connected to dramatic action
Applies at least one relevant convention
Explains how each choice shapes the drama — not just describes what was done

nodes.label: Using feedback to develop and refine drama
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use feedback, reflection and evaluation to develop and extend ideas when improvising, devising or interpreting drama
nodes.minimum_width: Use at least one piece of feedback to make a specific change to own drama; explain what the feedback revealed and what changed
nodes.typical_width: Use feedback, reflection and evaluation throughout the devising or interpreting process; document how each round of feedback develops and extends the drama
wider: Use Viewpoints questions to evaluate own drama in progress — 'What are the intentions in the drama?', 'Is meaning clear?', 'How could elements be used differently?' — document how the questions direct development
Develop a devising journal that documents how feedback and reflection have shaped dramatic decisions across a unit
Evaluate own devising process against the intended dramatic purpose — identify moments where feedback changed the direction and evaluate whether the change improved the drama

response_modes.reason: Using feedback and reflection to genuinely develop drama — rather than just acknowledging it — requires sustained practice with the feedback cycle. Students who engage with one round of feedback without iterating haven't built the habit that makes reflection productive. The skill develops through iteration.

This node brings together dramatic potential identification (Node 1), element manipulation and convention application (Node 2), and reflective practice from D02 into a complete devising and evaluation cycle. Students who can make dramatic choices but cannot use feedback to develop them are missing the integration that makes the drama a sustained creative act.

success_criteria: Uses at least one piece of feedback to make a specific documented change
Explains what the feedback revealed and what changed
Reflection is connected to dramatic intent — not just general improvement
